hero.title: Can AI Generate Game Audio in Real-Time?
hero.subtitle: I spent months finding out. The answer surprised me.

whyThisMatters.title: Why Would Anyone Want This?
whyThisMatters.description: Imagine a game where every gunshot sounds unique. Every footstep adapts to the surface. No two explosions are identical. That's the promise of AI audio.

variation.title: Infinite Variation
variation.description: Traditional games ship with 5-10 gunshot samples. Players hear the same sounds loop. AI could generate unique variations every time.

fileSize.title: Smaller Games
fileSize.description: AAA games ship with gigabytes of audio files. What if we could generate them on-the-fly instead of storing 500 WAV files?

adaptive.title: Adaptive Audio
adaptive.description: Sound that reacts to context. A gun sounds different in a cave vs. outdoors. AI could adapt in real-time to the environment.

whyThisMatters.hook: Sounds amazing, right? There's just one problem...

latency.title: The Latency Problem
latency.description: Shoot a gun in a game. If the bang comes 100 milliseconds late, your brain notices. That tiny gap breaks immersion. Now imagine waiting 12 seconds for each sound.

chart.title: The Numbers Don't Lie
chart.subtitle: I tested three AI audio models. Here's how they compare to what games actually need.

tooltip.elevenlabs: Cloud API. Best quality, but latency varies wildly based on server load.
tooltip.mmaudio: Video-to-audio model. I adapted it for game use. Runs locally.
tooltip.audiogen: Meta's text-to-audio. Balanced, but still too slow for real-time.
tooltip.cached: Pre-generated sounds played from memory. This is the breakthrough.

models.title: What I Actually Tested
models.subtitle: Three models, hundreds of tests, one Unity prototype. Here's what I found.
models.elevenlabs_note: Cloud-based. Amazing quality, but you're at the mercy of their servers. I saw 1-second responses and 12-second responses on the same day.
models.mmaudio_note: Originally designed for video soundtracks. I hacked it to work with game events. Surprisingly good ambient sounds.
models.audiogen_note: Meta's model. Most consistent, but 3 seconds is still 3 seconds too slow for a gunshot.

timeline.title: The Research Journey
timeline.subtitle: Four months of experiments, bugs, and late-night debugging sessions.

start.title: First Connection
start.description: Got Unity talking to Python via WebSocket. Simple prompt: 'gunshot'. Waited 8 seconds. Heard a terrible sound. But it worked!

models.title: Testing All Three Models
models.description: ElevenLabs had the best quality but was inconsistent. MMAudio was stable but slower. AudioGen was... okay. None were fast enough.

frustration.title: The Wall
frustration.description: Tried everything. Different prompts. Smaller audio files. Lower quality settings. Nothing got below 1 second. I thought the thesis was dead.

eureka.title: 3 AM Discovery
eureka.description: Checking server logs, I noticed something weird. Cache hits showed 0.03ms. Not 3ms. 0.03ms. The bottleneck wasn't AI - it was waiting for AI.

breakthrough.title: The 0.03ms Anomaly
breakthrough.subtitle: At 3 AM, staring at server logs, I found something that changed everything.
breakthrough.story: I was about to give up. Then I noticed a log line I'd been ignoring: 'cache_hit: 0.03ms'. I had added caching as an afterthought - just to avoid re-generating the same sound twice. But that number... 0.03 milliseconds. That's 40,000 times faster than generating a new sound.
breakthrough.realization: The problem wasn't making AI faster. The problem was calling AI at the wrong time.

cachingDiagram.title: The Solution: Generate Early, Play Instantly
cachingDiagram.subtitle: If we can't make AI fast, we make it invisible.

loading.label: Loading Screen
loading.description: While the player waits, AI generates sounds in the background

play.label: Player Acts
play.description: Bang! Sound plays from cache in under 50ms

refill.label: Background Refill
refill.description: AI quietly generates replacement sounds for next time

solution.title: Before & After
solution.subtitle: Same sounds. Same quality. Completely different experience.
solution.quote: We don't need to be fast. We just need to be early.

useCases.title: So When Can We Actually Use This?
useCases.subtitle: AI audio isn't magic. It's a tool with specific use cases.

footsteps.name: Footsteps
footsteps.note: Too frequent. Cache empties faster than AI can fill it.

ambient.name: Ambient Sounds
ambient.note: Perfect. Background sounds can be pre-generated during loading.

gunshots.name: Gunshots
gunshots.note: Works if you limit fire rate or use hybrid cache + fallback.

cutscenes.name: Cutscene Audio
cutscenes.note: Best case. You know exactly what's needed ahead of time.

procedural.name: Procedural Music
procedural.note: Possible with segment-based generation. Still experimental.

conclusion.main: AI audio isn't ready to replace traditional game audio.
conclusion.secondary: But with predictive caching, it's ready to enhance it. The technology will only get faster.
conclusion.final_thought: In 2-3 years? Real-time AI audio might actually be possible. For now, we work with what we have.
